items.content: The fireflies came out just after dusk, blinking their cold green light across the tall grass as if the field itself were dreaming. She stood at the edge of it, barefoot in the cooling earth, watching them rise and fade and rise again. There was something unbearable about their beauty — the way it arrived without warning at the end of August, when everything worth keeping was already preparing to leave.

items.content: The train lurches forward with a groan, pressing bodies together like pages in a closed book. Fluorescent light flickers overhead, casting everyone in the same pale, unflattering mercy. A woman clutches a paper coffee cup as though it were something sacred, her eyes fixed on the middle distance where strangers agree not to look at one another. The smell of wet wool and ambition fills the car. Outside, the tunnel darkness rushes past, indifferent and absolute.

items.content: The house breathes differently when everyone has gone. It settles into itself — the creak of a floorboard cooling, the refrigerator humming its low, indifferent note — as though it has been waiting all along for exactly this. Cups still hold the warmth of morning. A coat hangs by the door like a forgotten intention. There is something almost sacred in it, this silence that belongs to no one, that asks nothing, that simply remains.
